Lecture 10

Systems through elimination and integrable combinations

Lecture objectives

We count the initial data and the free constants of a linear system with continuous coefficients, and we pass between higher-order equations and first-order systems. We solve two-component systems by elimination and by integrable combinations, recover every component and check the result in every original equation.

Lecture 7 rewrote a second-order linear equation as a first-order system for the value and the slope. Many physical models are systems from the start. The amounts of salt in connected tanks, the velocity components of a charged particle and the temperatures of two bodies in thermal contact each obey several coupled equations. In this lecture we formulate such systems with their initial data and solve small linear systems by two elementary methods. Elimination turns two equations into one second-order equation. Integrable combinations are equations, obtained by combining the equations of a system, that can be solved on their own.

10.1 Systems and their initial data

From now on the independent variable is the time t,tt, and a dot denotes the derivative in t.tt. Lecture 7 used xxx for the independent variable and u\vv uu for the unknown vector. In Lectures 10–14 the bold letter x\vv xx denotes the unknown vector, with components x1,…,xn,x_1,\dots,x_nx1​,…,xn​, as usual for the state of a physical system. The letter III denotes the identity matrix, and JJJ is an open interval of times.

Definition 10.1 (First-order system). Let D⊂R×RnD\subset\R\times\R^nD⊂R×Rn be open and F:D→Rn\vv F:D\to\R^nF:D→Rn continuous. The equation x˙=F(t,x)\dot{\vv x}=\vv F(t,\vv x)x˙=F(t,x)(10.1) is a first-order system of nnn equations. A solution on an open interval (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)(α,β) is a C1C^1C1 function x:(α,β)→Rn\vv x:(\alpha,\beta)\to\R^nx:(α,β)→Rn with (t,x(t))∈D(t,\vv x(t))\in D(t,x(t))∈D and x˙(t)=F(t,x(t))\dot{\vv x}(t)=\vv F(t,\vv x(t))x˙(t)=F(t,x(t)) for every t∈(α,β).t\in(\alpha,\beta)t∈(α,β). An initial-value problem adds the condition x(t0)=x0\vv x(t_0)=\vv x_0x(t0​)=x0​ for a point (t0,x0)∈D.(t_0,\vv x_0)\in D(t0​,x0​)∈D.

The system has nnn unknown functions, and its initial data are nnn numbers. The existence theorem of Lecture 4 has a version for systems. If the partial derivatives of F\vv FF in the components of x\vv xx exist and are continuous on D,DD, each initial-value problem has a unique maximal solution (Teschl, Theorems 2.2 and 2.13 and Corollary 2.16). The continuous partial derivatives give a local Lipschitz condition, by the mean value theorem applied to each component along a segment, as in Lecture 4. Lecture 6 used this version with n=2.n=2n=2.

The linear system of Lecture 7 has F(t,x)=A(t)x+b(t),\vv F(t,\vv x)=A(t)\vv x+\vv b(t)F(t,x)=A(t)x+b(t), that is, x˙=A(t)x+b(t),\dot{\vv x}=A(t)\vv x+\vv b(t),x˙=A(t)x+b(t),(10.2) with an n×nn\times nn×n matrix AAA and a vector b\vv bb whose entries are continuous on J.JJ. The system is homogeneous if b=0\vv b=0b=0 on J.JJ. By the existence and uniqueness theorem of Lecture 7, for every t0∈Jt_0\in Jt0​∈J and x0∈Rn\vv x_0\in\R^nx0​∈Rn the system (10.2) has exactly one solution on all of JJJ with x(t0)=x0.\vv x(t_0)=\vv x_0x(t0​)=x0​. This fixes the number of free constants in a formula that contains all solutions.

Theorem 10.2 (Counting constants). Let AAA and b\vv bb be continuous on J,JJ, and let t0∈J.t_0\in Jt0​∈J.

  • The solutions on JJJ of the homogeneous system x˙=A(t)x\dot{\vv x}=A(t)\vv xx˙=A(t)x form a vector space S.SS. The map S→RnS\to\R^nS→Rn given by x↦x(t0)\vv x\mapsto\vv x(t_0)x↦x(t0​) is a linear bijection, so dim⁡S=n.\dim S=ndimS=n.

  • Let x(1),…,x(n)∈S,\vv x^{(1)},\dots,\vv x^{(n)}\in Sx(1),…,x(n)∈S, and let xp\vv x_{\mathrm p}xp​ solve (10.2) on J.JJ. Consider the family x=xp+c1x(1)+⋯+cnx(n),c1,…,cn∈R.\vv x=\vv x_{\mathrm p}+c_1\vv x^{(1)}+\dots+c_n\vv x^{(n)},\qquad c_1,\dots,c_n\in\R.x=xp​+c1​x(1)+⋯+cn​x(n),c1​,…,cn​∈R.(10.3) The vectors x(1)(t0),…,x(n)(t0)\vv x^{(1)}(t_0),\dots,\vv x^{(n)}(t_0)x(1)(t0​),…,x(n)(t0​) are linearly independent if and only if the family contains every solution of (10.2) on JJJ and different constants give different solutions.

Proof. First, the solutions of the homogeneous system form the kernel of the linear map x↦x˙−Ax,\vv x\mapsto\dot{\vv x}-A\vv xx↦x˙−Ax, so they form a vector space. The map x↦x(t0)\vv x\mapsto\vv x(t_0)x↦x(t0​) is linear. It is surjective by the existence theorem, and injective because a solution with the value 000 at t0t_0t0​ is the zero solution by uniqueness. This is the argument of the dimension theorem of Lecture 7.

Next, let MMM be the n×nn\times nn×n matrix with the columns x(j)(t0)\vv x^{(j)}(t_0)x(j)(t0​) and put c=(c1,…,cn).\vv c=(c_1,\dots,c_n)c=(c1​,…,cn​). The member (10.3) with constants c\vv cc solves (10.2), because its derivative is Axp+b+∑jcjAx(j).A\vv x_{\mathrm p}+\vv b+\sum_jc_jA\vv x^{(j)}Axp​+b+∑j​cj​Ax(j). Its value at t0t_0t0​ is xp(t0)+Mc.\vv x_{\mathrm p}(t_0)+M\vv cxp​(t0​)+Mc. By uniqueness a solution is determined by its value at t0.t_0t0​. Hence the family contains every solution exactly when every vector of Rn\R^nRn has the form xp(t0)+Mc,\vv x_{\mathrm p}(t_0)+M\vv cxp​(t0​)+Mc, that is, when MMM is surjective. Two constant vectors give the same solution exactly when they give the same value at t0.t_0t0​. So different constants give different solutions exactly when MMM is injective. For a square matrix both properties are equivalent to linearly independent columns (GM 22). ■

Definition 10.3 (General solution of a linear system). A family (10.3) whose terms x(j)\vv x^{(j)}x(j) are solutions of the homogeneous system with linearly independent values at some t0∈Jt_0\in Jt0​∈J is the general solution of (10.2).

The point t0t_0t0​ in the theorem is arbitrary, so values that are independent at one time are independent at every time. Lecture 7 defined the general solution of a scalar second-order equation in the same way. The nnn constants correspond one to one to the nnn initial data. A family with fewer than nnn constants misses solutions. In a family of the form (10.3) with more than nnn homogeneous terms, some different constants give the same solution, because more than nnn vectors in Rn\R^nRn are linearly dependent. Such constants are not independent.

10.2 Higher-order equations as systems

A scalar linear equation of order n,nn, y(n)+an−1(t)y(n−1)+⋯+a1(t)y˙+a0(t)y=f(t),y^{(n)}+a_{n-1}(t)y^{(n-1)}+\dots+a_1(t)\dot y+a_0(t)y=f(t),y(n)+an−1​(t)y(n−1)+⋯+a1​(t)y˙​+a0​(t)y=f(t),(10.4) with a0,…,an−1a_0,\dots,a_{n-1}a0​,…,an−1​ and fff continuous on J,JJ, needs the nnn data y(t0),y˙(t0),…,y(n−1)(t0).y(t_0),\dot y(t_0),\dots,y^{(n-1)}(t_0)y(t0​),y˙​(t0​),…,y(n−1)(t0​). As in Lecture 7, we collect the unknown and its first n−1n-1n−1 derivatives in the state vector x=(yy˙⋮y(n−1)),A=(010⋯0001⋯0⋮⋱⋮000⋯1−a0−a1−a2⋯−an−1),b=(0⋮0f).\vv x=\begin{pmatrix}y\\\dot y\\\vdots\\y^{(n-1)}\end{pmatrix},\qquad A=\begin{pmatrix} 0&1&0&\cdots&0\\ 0&0&1&\cdots&0\\ \vdots&&&\ddots&\vdots\\ 0&0&0&\cdots&1\\ -a_0&-a_1&-a_2&\cdots&-a_{n-1} \end{pmatrix},\qquad \vv b=\begin{pmatrix}0\\\vdots\\0\\f\end{pmatrix}.x=​yy˙​⋮y(n−1)​​,A=​00⋮0−a0​​100−a1​​010−a2​​⋯⋯⋱⋯⋯​00⋮1−an−1​​​,b=​0⋮0f​​.(10.5) The first n−1n-1n−1 rows of x˙=Ax+b\dot{\vv x}=A\vv x+\vv bx˙=Ax+b say x˙k=xk+1.\dot x_k=x_{k+1}x˙k​=xk+1​. The last row is the equation (10.4). The matrix AAA is the companion matrix of the equation.

If y∈Cn(J)y\in C^n(J)y∈Cn(J) solves (10.4), then x\vv xx solves the system. Conversely, let x\vv xx solve the system and put y=x1.y=x_1y=x1​. The rows x˙k=xk+1\dot x_k=x_{k+1}x˙k​=xk+1​ show, one after another, that yyy is CnC^nCn with y(k)=xk+1y^{(k)}=x_{k+1}y(k)=xk+1​ for k<n.k<nk<n. The last row then becomes (10.4). By this equivalence and the existence and uniqueness theorem of Lecture 7 for the system, each initial-value problem for (10.4) has exactly one solution on J.JJ. By the counting theorem, the homogeneous equation has an nnn-dimensional space of solutions. A nonlinear equation y(n)=g(t,y,…,y(n−1))y^{(n)}=g(t,y,\dots,y^{(n-1)})y(n)=g(t,y,…,y(n−1)) becomes the system (10.1) with F=(x2,…,xn,g)\vv F=(x_2,\dots,x_n,g)F=(x2​,…,xn​,g) in the same way.

Lectures 11–13 return to this system. ◃

Elimination goes the other way. It turns a system into a single equation of higher order for one of the unknowns. The next section carries it out for two equations.

The left side of (10.8) has the characteristic polynomial χ(λ)=λ2−(tr⁡A)λ+det⁡A.\chi(\lambda)=\lambda^2-(\tr A)\lambda+\det Aχ(λ)=λ2−(trA)λ+detA. It equals det⁡(λI−A),\det(\lambda I-A)det(λI−A), and Lecture 11 meets it again as the characteristic polynomial of the matrix A.AA.

The proposition also transfers the data. The values x1(t0)x_1(t_0)x1​(t0​) and x2(t0)x_2(t_0)x2​(t0​) give the data of the eliminated equation, x1(t0),x˙1(t0)=a11x1(t0)+a12x2(t0)+b1(t0).x_1(t_0),\qquad \dot x_1(t_0)=a_{11}x_1(t_0)+a_{12}x_2(t_0)+b_1(t_0).x1​(t0​),x˙1​(t0​)=a11​x1​(t0​)+a12​x2​(t0​)+b1​(t0​).(10.10) The equation (10.8) has constant coefficients. Lectures 7 and 8 give its general solution with two free constants, and these are fixed by (10.10). The reconstruction (10.9) involves no integration, so it adds no constant. Two constants for two data agree with the counting theorem.

If a12=0,a_{12}=0a12​=0, the system is triangular. The first equation contains only x1,x_1x1​, and it is a first-order linear equation, solved as in Lecture 5. The second is then a first-order linear equation for x2x_2x2​ with a known forcing. No elimination is needed.

For more than two equations, elimination produces equations of higher order and reconstruction formulas with several derivatives. The bookkeeping grows quickly, and Lecture 11 replaces it by matrix methods.

A frequent error is to eliminate twice, once for each unknown, and to solve the two eliminated equations independently. This produces four constants for two data.

10.4 Two connected tanks

The first model is a homogeneous system with real characteristic roots. Figure 10.1 shows the arrangement.

10.5 An inhomogeneous system: crossed fields

The second model has a constant forcing and complex characteristic roots. A proton of mass mmm and charge e>0e>0e>0 moves in a uniform magnetic field B=Be^3\vv B=B\unitvec3B=Be3​ and a uniform electric field E=Ee^2,\vv E=E\unitvec2E=Ee2​, with B>0B>0B>0 and E>0.E>0E>0. 10.6 Integrable combinations

Sometimes the equations of a system can be combined into one equation that the methods of Lectures 4 and 5 solve.

Definition 10.9 (Integrable combination). An integrable combination of a system is a solvable scalar differential equation obtained from its equations by addition, subtraction, multiplication and division.

The solution of an integrable combination is a relation Φ(t,x)=c\Phi(t,\vv x)=cΦ(t,x)=c that holds along every solution of the system on each time interval on which the solution stays where the operations used to form the combination are defined. Solutions on a set excluded by a division are checked separately, as the lost solutions of Lecture 4 were.

Definition 10.10 (First integral). Let DDD and F\vv FF be as in Definition 10.1. A C1C^1C1 function Φ:D→R\Phi:D\to\RΦ:D→R is a first integral of the system (10.1) if t↦Φ(t,x(t))t\mapsto\Phi(t,\vv x(t))t↦Φ(t,x(t)) is constant for every solution x.\vv xx.

This extends the notion of Lecture 4 from one equation to systems, without the condition ∂yΦ≠0\partial_y\Phi\ne0∂y​Φ=0 used there. By the chain rule, the derivative of Φ(t,x(t))\Phi(t,\vv x(t))Φ(t,x(t)) along a solution is ∂tΦ+∑iFi ∂xiΦ,\partial_t\Phi+\sum_iF_i\,\partial_{x_i}\Phi∂t​Φ+∑i​Fi​∂xi​​Φ, evaluated at (t,x(t)).(t,\vv x(t))(t,x(t)). So Φ\PhiΦ is a first integral if this expression vanishes on D.DD. Where ∂xiΦ≠0,\partial_{x_i}\Phi\ne0∂xi​​Φ=0, the relation Φ=c\Phi=cΦ=c can be solved for xix_ixi​ near each such point by the implicit function theorem (GM 37). Each such first integral removes one unknown. Similarly, nnn first integrals Φ1,…,Φn\Phi_1,\dots,\Phi_nΦ1​,…,Φn​ whose matrix of partial derivatives ∂xiΦk\partial_{x_i}\Phi_k∂xi​​Φk​ is invertible determine x\vv xx near each such point.

The sum and the difference of the two equations are  ⁣d ⁣dt(x1+x2)=x1+x2, ⁣d ⁣dt(x1−x2)=−(x1−x2).\frac{\dd}{\dd t}(x_1+x_2)=x_1+x_2,\qquad \frac{\dd}{\dd t}(x_1-x_2)=-(x_1-x_2).dtd​(x1​+x2​)=x1​+x2​,dtd​(x1​−x2​)=−(x1​−x2​). Two constants appear, as the counting theorem requires. The first integrals are Φ1=e−t(x1+x2)\Phi_1=\ee^{-t}(x_1+x_2)Φ1​=e−t(x1​+x2​) and Φ2=et(x1−x2).\Phi_2=\ee^t(x_1-x_2)Φ2​=et(x1​−x2​). For a particle with the potential energy VVV of Lecture 6, the system q˙=p/m,\dot q=p/mq˙​=p/m, p˙=−V′(q)\dot p=-V'(q)p˙​=−V′(q) for the position and the momentum gives, after multiplying the first equation by V′(q)V'(q)V′(q) and the second by p/mp/mp/m and adding,  ⁣d ⁣dt(p2/(2m)+V(q))=0.\frac{\dd}{\dd t}\bigl(p^2/(2m)+V(q)\bigr)=0dtd​(p2/(2m)+V(q))=0. This is the energy integral of Lecture 6.

Linear integrable combinations

For a linear system with a constant matrix AAA integrable combinations of a linear kind are found by linear algebra. We write α=(α1,…,αn)\vv\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)α=(α1​,…,αn​) for a row of numbers, so that αx=α1x1+⋯+αnxn\vv\alpha\vv x=\alpha_1x_1+\dots+\alpha_nx_nαx=α1​x1​+⋯+αn​xn​ and αA\vv\alpha AαA is again a row.

Definition 10.12 (Linear integrable combination). Let AAA be a constant n×nn\times nn×n matrix. A nonzero row α,\vv\alphaα, with real or complex entries, gives a linear integrable combination of the system (10.2) if there is a number μ\muμ with αA=μα.\vv\alpha A=\mu\vv\alpha.αA=μα.(10.15) The combination is then the equation z˙=μz+αb(t)\dot z=\mu z+\vv\alpha\vv b(t)z˙=μz+αb(t) for the function z=αx.z=\vv\alpha\vv xz=αx.

For complex μ\muμ that proof uses the derivative μeμt\mu\ee^{\mu t}μeμt of eμt\ee^{\mu t}eμt (GM 16), the product rule and the fundamental theorem of calculus. Summary

A first-order system of nnn equations needs nnn initial data. For a linear system with continuous coefficients the homogeneous solutions form an nnn-dimensional space, and the general solution has exactly nnn independent constants. A scalar equation of order nnn is equivalent to a system for its state vector. Conversely, a two-component system with a constant matrix, a12≠0a_{12}\ne0a12​=0 and b1∈C1b_1\in C^1b1​∈C1 is equivalent to one second-order equation for x1x_1x1​ together with an algebraic formula for x2.x_2x2​. That formula adds no constant. An integrable combination is a solvable equation obtained by combining the equations of a system. Its solution is a relation Φ=c,\Phi=cΦ=c, where Φ\PhiΦ is constant along every solution that stays in the open set where the combination is defined. For a constant matrix, a row with αA=μα\vv\alpha A=\mu\vv\alphaαA=μα gives a linear integrable combination: the function αx\vv\alpha\vv xαx obeys a scalar first-order equation, and nnn independent rows determine the solution. Every component of a solution is checked in every original equation and initial condition.

  • Counting constants: for AAA and b\vv bb continuous on J,JJ, the general solution of x˙=Ax+b\dot{\vv x}=A\vv x+\vv bx˙=Ax+b has nnn independent constants, one for each datum.

  • Companion system: the state vector (y,y˙,…,y(n−1))(y,\dot y,\dots,y^{(n-1)})(y,y˙​,…,y(n−1)) turns an equation of order nnn into a first-order system.

  • Elimination: for constant AAA with a12≠0a_{12}\ne0a12​=0 and b1∈C1,b_1\in C^1b1​∈C1, x¨1−(tr⁡A)x˙1+(det⁡A)x1=b˙1−a22b1+a12b2\ddot x_1-(\tr A)\dot x_1+(\det A)x_1=\dot b_1-a_{22}b_1+a_{12}b_2x¨1​−(trA)x˙1​+(detA)x1​=b˙1​−a22​b1​+a12​b2​ and x2=(x˙1−a11x1−b1)/a12.x_2=(\dot x_1-a_{11}x_1-b_1)/a_{12}x2​=(x˙1​−a11​x1​−b1​)/a12​.

  • First integral: a function Φ(t,x)\Phi(t,\vv x)Φ(t,x) that is constant along every solution.

  • Linear integrable combination: for constant A,AA, if αA=μα\vv\alpha A=\mu\vv\alphaαA=μα then z=αxz=\vv\alpha\vv xz=αx satisfies z˙=μz+αb;\dot z=\mu z+\vv\alpha\vv bz˙=μz+αb; μ\muμ is a root of det⁡(μI−A).\det(\mu I-A)det(μI−A).

3. For the system x˙1=−2x1+x2\dot x_1=-2x_1+x_2x˙1​=−2x1​+x2​, x˙2=2x1−x2\dot x_2=2x_1-x_2x˙2​=2x1​−x2​, which combination is constant along every solution?

Hint. Differentiate the combinations using both equations. Look for cancellation for arbitrary initial values.

The right-hand sides are opposites, so the derivative of x1+x2x_1+x_2x1​+x2​ is zero. The derivative of x1−x2x_1-x_2x1​−x2​ is −4x1+2x2-4x_1+2x_2−4x1​+2x2​. The derivative of x1+2x2x_1+2x_2x1​+2x2​ is 2x1−x22x_1-x_22x1​−x2​, and that of 2x1+x22x_1+x_22x1​+x2​ is −2x1+x2-2x_1+x_2−2x1​+x2​. These vanish on the equilibrium line only, so the other combinations are not first integrals for all initial data.

4. For a regular two-component linear system with continuous forcing, a particular solution is known. What must be checked to justify a proposed general solution built by adding two constant multiples of vector functions to that particular solution?

Hint. A general solution must satisfy the system for every choice of constants and reach every initial state.

Subtracting the particular solution leaves a homogeneous solution. Two homogeneous solutions with independent initial vectors span all initial differences, and uniqueness makes the resulting solutions exhaustive. Two written constants can represent just one direction. Adding forced solutions generally changes the forcing, and checking an eliminated scalar equation alone does not establish that the full vectors satisfy both equations.
